title: Structural and Thermodynamic Investigation of Glycated Hemoglobin: β-Val1–Heme Connectivity, Allosteric Oxygen-Unloading Regulation, and the Glycohypoxia Hypothesis
content: Background: Hemoglobin β-Val1 glycation may influence oxygen binding through altered electrostatics, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) interactions, conformational redistribution, or heme electronic perturbation. We investigated these mechanisms and their potential relevance to the Glycohypoxia hypothesis. Methods: We performed crystallographic reanalysis of PDB 3B75, 2DN1, and 2DN2; Cα structural superposition; 4.5-Å residue-contact network analysis; and exploratory MMFF94 optimization of valine and fructosyl-valine fragments. Published nonglycated QM/MM oxygen-binding energies and experimental oxygen- and BPG-affinity ratios were quantitatively reanalyzed. Affinity ratios were converted to standard binding free-energy equivalents assuming 310.15 K. Results: PDB 3B75 contained three glucose and two fructose ligands but no explicitly modeled covalent fructosyl-Val1 adduct; the nearest N-terminal nitrogen–carbohydrate separation was approximately 10.4 Å. Across five β chains, oxygenated-reference Cα RMSDs were 0.383–0.670 Å, deoxygenated-reference RMSDs were 0.687–0.951 Å, and β-Val1–heme-iron distances were 19.425–20.119 Å. Contact networks contained 653–682 edges and 19–22 heme-adjacent residues. Two-edge geometric paths involved Val1–Leu81–Phe85 (four chains) or Val1–Val133–Val137 (one chain). Published QM/MM R-minus-T electronic-energy contrasts were −7.1 kcal/mol (α) and −9.0 kcal/mol (β). A reported tenfold oxygen-affinity increase corresponded to −1.419 kcal/mol; 2.6- and 1.7-fold BPG-affinity reductions corresponded to +0.589 and +0.327 kcal/mol, respectively. Thirty conformers per molecular fragment were successfully optimized. Conclusions: β-Val1 glycation may influence oxygen binding through central-cavity electrostatics, BPG-dependent allostery, and conformational redistribution, with direct heme electronic effects remaining untested. Static structural connectivity and affinity-derived energetic equivalents do not establish glycation-specific molecular causality or impaired tissue oxygenation. These findings provide a quantitative framework for testing Glycohypoxia.
